accepted.summary:
Both halves of FIX-1 implemented in /home/user/browser-use-/.claude/worktrees/wf_bd8e1eb2-305-4.

(a) Resolver/scanner test-id parity. scanner.py:113 folds three attributes into one `testid` field (`data-testid || data-test-id || data-test`) and, once it has one, deliberately computes no CSS fallback. RESOLVE_JS only queried the first two, so an element carrying only `data-test` with no id and no accessible name resolved to `{found:false}` — its tool answered 'could not find' on every call and could never reach `_mark_verified`. Added the third `deepQuery('[data-test="..."]')[0]` branch in the same order, and rewrote the comment above it to state the parity requirement and why a missing branch is fatal rather than merely degraded.

(b) Fill replaces instead of appends. `call()` ran `human.click_box(rect)` then `human.type_text(value)`; keystrokes insert at the caret, so a pre-filled field yielded 'oldnew' (confirmed empirically — the pre-fix run asserts exactly `'oldnew' == 'new'`) while still returning ok=True and marking the tool verified. Added `SELECT_CONTENTS_JS`, a resolver variant built through the existing `_variant()` machinery, that does `el.focus(); el.select()` for input/textarea (wrapped in try/catch for input types with no selectable text) and a `Range.selectNodeContents` for contenteditable, taking the selection from `el.getRootNode()` when that root exposes `getSelection` so a contenteditable inside a shadow root works. It is driven by a new `_select_contents()` that goes through `_fill(..., LOCATOR_JSON=_encode(locator))`, so page data still passes only through `_encode`/`_fill` and the single-pass injection guarantee is untouched. It is called between click_box and type_text in 'fill' steps only; 'select' steps stay on SELECT_JS, and the `value in (None, '')` skip is unchanged. A field it cannot select is still typed into (appending to an empty field is filling it), so no common case regresses.

accepted.title: WebMCP call_tool runs a stale synthesized tool instead of the page's own declared tool
accepted.summary:
Fixed FIX-4: WebMCPService.call_tool() (browser_use/webmcp/service.py) was routing calls through the synthesizer's per-origin manifest cache (self.synthesizer.cached(origin)) whenever synthesize_site_tools was on, without checking whether the latest discover() pass for this target still considers the tool synthesized. Since discover() only re-synthesizes when a page declares nothing, a page that registers its own tool of the same name after an earlier synthesized scan (SPA registering post-load, or a same-origin nav) left the synthesizer's stale manifest still containing the old synthesized tool, so call_tool kept driving the old UI steps instead of the page's real declared handler.

Fix: before taking the synthesized branch, look up self._cache.get(cdp_session.target_id) (the WebMCPService's own per-target discovery cache, populated by discover()) and only proceed down the synthesized path when that cache lists the requested tool name with source == 'synthesized'. Otherwise execution falls through to the normal bridge call, which invokes whatever the page currently declares. Also switched synthesizer.call(...) to pass cdp_session.target_id (the resolved target) instead of the raw, possibly-None target_id parameter, per the work item's instructions. discover() itself was left untouched.

Added a regression test tests/ci/test_webmcp_declared_precedence.py using the shared module-scoped webmcp_session fixture (BrowserProfile(enable_webmcp=True), synthesize_site_tools defaults True) and a pytest-httpserver page with a search form plus a setTimeout(..., 1000) that registers navigator.modelContext.registerTool({name: 'search', ...}) returning 'declared:'+q. The test: (1) navigates and calls get_webmcp_tools() once, asserting the synthesized 'search' tool is discovered from the form; (2) sleeps past the 1s registration, discovers again, and asserts the tool is now source == 'js'; (3) calls call_webmcp_tool('search', {'q': 'x'}) and asserts result.content == 'declared:x'; (4) asserts window.__formUsed was never set to true, proving the old synthesized UI-driving path did not run. This test fails against the pre-fix code (which would run the synthesized form-fill/submit path since the synthesizer's origin-level manifest cache never gets invalidated by the later declaration) and passes with the fix.

Note: this worker instance only implements the single assigned bug-fix work item (FIX-4) in this isolated worktree, per the harness's computed task. accepted.title: Human input: a cancelled hold, press_and_hold, click or keystroke leaves the key or mouse button stuck down
accepted.summary:
Confirmed bug and fixed it. In `browser_use/human/input.py` every down/up pair (`click`, `type_text`, `press`, `hold`, `press_and_hold`) awaited a sleep between the down event and the up event with no cleanup. An agent step timeout cancels the task mid-sleep — which is where nearly all the wall time in those methods lives — so `CancelledError` is thrown at the sleep, the coroutine unwinds, and the matching `keyUp`/`mouseReleased` is never dispatched. The Python task dies but the renderer never hears about it: Blink and the page keep the key or button held, so the next action types into a browser still holding ArrowRight, or drags instead of clicking, with nothing in the logs explaining it.

Fix: each down…up pair is now `try: <sleep> finally: await self._release(...)`, with the release sent using exactly the same params as before. `_release` is a new static helper that awaits the send, re-raises `asyncio.CancelledError` unchanged (swallowing it would make these methods uncancellable), and catches only `Exception` into a `logger.debug` — so a dead CDP session or a navigated-away page cannot replace the exception already propagating. Timing, jitter, auto-repeat cadence and the normal-path event order are untouched; the release simply moved into the `finally` that already runs on the happy path.

Note on scope: `move_to` and `wheel` are unchanged — neither leaves state latched in the renderer when interrupted, so wrapping them would add noise without fixing anything.

Regression test `tests/ci/test_human_input_cancellation.py` serves a pytest-httpserver page that records every keydown/keyup/mousedown/mouseup into `window.__log` and reads it back with `run_page_script`:
1. `hold('ArrowRight', 5)` cancelled ~0.4s in — raises `CancelledError`, last ArrowRight event must be `keyup`. Fails before the fix (last event is an auto-repeat `keydown`).
2. `press_and_hold(box, 5)` cancelled the same way — last button0 event must be `mouseup`. Fails before the fix (no `mouseup` at all).
3. An uncancelled `hold('ArrowLeft', 0.3)` still ends in exactly one `keyup` and still auto-repeats, guarding against the cleanup path double-releasing or displacing the happy path.

Both cancellation tests wait for the page to actually observe the down event before cancelling, so a slow CDP round trip during pointer travel cannot make the test pass for the wrong reason. No virtualenv here, so the suite was not run — `tests/ci/test_human_input.py` is untouched and its normal-path event sequences are unchanged by construction.

+
+Every hold in `browser_use.human.input` is a sleep between a down event and an up event,
+and the agent cancels its step task on timeout — mid-sleep, most of the time, because the
+sleep is where the time goes. The Python task dies; the renderer does not hear about it.

+still holding ArrowRight, or drags instead of clicking, and nothing in the logs says why.
+

+assertion is on the last event for that key or button: it has to be the release.
+"""

+import json
+
+import pytest
+from pytest_httpserver import HTTPServer
+
+from browser_use.browser.events import NavigateToUrlEvent
+from browser_use.human import HumanInput
+

+# the last thing that happened to ArrowRight" is answerable.
+RECORDER = """<!DOCTYPE html>
+<html><head><title>Hold recorder</title>
+<style>
+	body { margin: 0; }
+	#box { position: absolute; left: 300px; top: 220px; width: 160px; height: 60px; background: #ccc; }
+</style></head>
+<body>
+	<div id="box">box</div>
+<script>
+	window.__log = [];
+	const rec = (kind, name) => window.__log.push([kind, name]);
+	addEventListener('keydown', e => rec('keydown', e.key), true);
+	addEventListener('keyup', e => rec('keyup', e.key), true);
+	addEventListener('mousedown', e => rec('mousedown', 'button' + e.button), true);
+	addEventListener('mouseup', e => rec('mouseup', 'button' + e.button), true);
+</script>
+</body></html>"""
+
+BOX = (300.0, 220.0, 160.0, 60.0)
+
+
+@pytest.fixture(scope='module')
+def hold_server():
+	server = HTTPServer()
+	server.start()
+	server.expect_request('/holds').respond_with_data(RECORDER, content_type='text/html')
+	yield server
+	server.stop()
+
+

+	event = session.event_bus.dispatch(NavigateToUrlEvent(url=url))
+	await event
+	await event.event_result(raise_if_any=True, raise_if_none=False)

+

accepted.title: Decide: parse_decisions raises on a malformed usage block (breaks the never-raises contract), and choose_tool can return a tool it never offered
accepted.summary:
FIX-7 confirmed as a real bug on both counts and fixed.

(1) `Jev.ask()` is documented "Never raises", but `parse_decisions` ran outside the try block and did `int(usage.get('input_tokens') or 0)` on whatever the server sent. Verified the three raising paths concretely: `int('n/a')` -> ValueError, `int(json.loads('1e400'))` -> OverflowError (JSON 1e400 decodes to float inf), `int([1])` -> TypeError. So a 200 OK with a junk usage block took down the agent step the decision model was supposed to be optimizing — exactly the dependency the module docstring swears it is not.

Fix: added `_count(value) -> int` which returns 0 for bools, non-numbers, negatives and non-finite floats. It checks `isinstance(value, int)` before touching `math.isfinite`, because `math.isfinite(10**400)` itself raises OverflowError (it coerces to float) — a large JSON integer is a legitimate finite count and is passed through. Added a backstop `try/except Exception` around the `parse_decisions` call in `ask()`, logging at debug and returning `Decisions()`. The deliberate `ValueError` for >MAX_QUESTIONS is untouched — it fires before the request and stays.

Also added `_finite(value) -> float | None` for confidence: inf clears every threshold and nan clears none, so `Answer.certain()` would have been reporting a verdict the model never gave. bools are rejected too (`True` previously became confidence 1.0, i.e. instantly certain). `float()` is wrapped for the huge-int OverflowError case.

(2) `choose_tool` returned any sufficiently confident answer without checking it against the options it offered. A choice is only meaningful over its own criteria set; a name outside it is a hallucinated tool that fails at call time. Added `if answer.value not in options: return None`, placed after the NO_TOOL check and before the certainty check so the debug log lines stay distinct. `options` is built from `page_tools.tools[:MAX_CHOICE_OPTIONS - 1]`, so a tool truncated out of the offer is also correctly rejected.

Validation: the task said there is no venv in this worktree, and there isn't — but the main checkout has one at /home/user/browser-use-/.venv, which I used read-only as an interpreter with cwd set to this worktree (confirmed `browser_use.decide.service.__file__` resolves to the worktree copy; nothing in the main checkout was touched). Against unfixed source: 5 of the 6 new tests FAIL, the 6th (`test_an_offered_tool_still_comes_back`) passes as the control that the membership check must not over-reject. With the fix: 18 passed across test_decide_robustness.py + test_decide.py. `ruff format` and `ruff check` clean.

One thing for the lead to decide, left alone deliberately as out of scope: `probabilities={str(k): float(v) ...}` in parse_decisions can still raise OverflowError on a JSON integer too large for a float. That path is now caught by the ask() backstop (and `test_a_parse_error_nobody_anticipated_is_still_an_empty_result` exercises exactly it), but it costs the whole response rather than one bogus probability. Routing probabilities through `_finite` too would be a two-line follow-up.

accepted.title: Profile (lower priority): the headless 'headful' user agent always claims Linux, contradicting navigator.platform on macOS/Windows
accepted.summary: Confirmed bug: `_headful_user_agent()` hardcoded `X11; Linux x86_64` regardless of host, so a headless macOS/Windows session shipped a UA that contradicts `navigator.platform`/`navigator.userAgentData` — a mismatch that is itself a stronger automation signal than the `HeadlessChrome` token it was trying to hide. Fix: added a pure module-level helper `_ua_os_token(system: str) -> str` in browser_use/browser/profile.py (Darwin -> 'Macintosh; Intel Mac OS X 10_15_7', Windows -> 'Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64', everything else -> 'X11; Linux x86_64'), imported `platform` at module top, and made `_headful_user_agent()` interpolate `_ua_os_token(platform.system())`. Nothing else changed; the Chrome-version derivation is untouched. New regression test tests/ci/test_profile_user_agent.py covers the helper mapping with explicit system strings (no monkeypatching), asserts `_headful_user_agent()` carries the host token and never 'HeadlessChrome', and — Linux-only via skipif — asserts get_args() emits exactly one `--user-agent=` flag containing 'X11; Linux x86_64'. Before the fix the file fails at import (`_ua_os_token` does not exist); after it passes. No existing tests touched: test_profile_args.py and test_browser_fingerprint.py only assert the Linux-host behaviour, which is unchanged on this host. Not run here (no venv in the worktree).

rejected.title: Scroll-independent fingerprint, covering form-less controls, plus the single SYNTHESIS_VERSION bump
rejected.reason:
1. BLOCKING: the new `shape` payload can wipe out synthesis entirely on the pages this fix is aimed at. SynthesisService.scan() (service.py:256-271) calls run_page_script with max_chars=60000. If the result is truncated it returns {}, so no tools at all get synthesized. The patch adds uncapped name lists to the scan result: up to 200 button names, 120 loose-control names, and up to 120 control names for each of up to 12 forms. clean() allows 120 chars per name, so the worst case is roughly 220k chars. Even on a realistic crowded page, `shape` adds kilobytes on top of a payload whose comment already calls out that one checkout page with two country selects clears the budget. So the patch turns "fingerprint drifts with scroll" into "a crowded page gets zero tools". Fix: collapse the shape to a small fixed-size value inside the page script. For example, build the same sorted parts (`form:<name>:<sorted control names>`, `button:<name>`, `control:<name>`) in JS, join them, and return a short digest such as a cyrb53/FNV hex string as `shape`. fingerprint() then mixes that string into its parts (views/toggles/tables/pagers stay as they are). The other option is to keep names but dedupe them and hard-cap the total length of `shape` well below the budget. Either way, add an assertion in the tall-page test that the scan did not come back empty, and keep the scroll-invariance assertion as it is.
2. With the digest approach, simplify the fingerprint() branches to match. SCAN_JS ships in the same package as fingerprint(), so a scan without `shape` only happens with hand-built dicts. Keeping the fallback branch is fine because it carries the form-less `controls` fix and the second test covers it. But update the docstring to describe what `shape` now contains.
3. Minor, not blocking on its own: CLAUDE.md asks for related test logic to be condensed into one file. Put these two tests in the existing tests/ci/test_site_synthesis.py (reusing its server and navigation helpers if it has them) instead of adding tests/ci/test_synthesis_fingerprint.py with a second `_goto` helper.
